principles.name: Put Customers First
principles.description: Succeed only when customers succeed. Earn their trust daily, understand their pain points, and deliver products they love.
evidence_signals: Names a specific customer and the problem that was solved for them
Changed priorities based on what customers actually needed
Measured success in customer outcomes

principles.name: Integrity Always
principles.description: Be open, honest and respectful. Speak up candidly even when uncomfortable, debate respectfully, and commit fully once a decision is made.
evidence_signals: Raised an unpopular concern openly and respectfully
Disagreed, then committed fully once the decision was made
Admits mistakes plainly

principles.name: Think Big
principles.description: Be ambitious with big goals, focus on what matters, innovate and take prudent risks to make a lasting impact and win.
evidence_signals: Pursued an ambitious goal beyond the obvious scope
Took a prudent, well-reasoned risk
Focused effort on the highest-impact problem

principles.name: Be Excellent
principles.description: Quality counts. Hold yourself and others to the highest standards, value simplicity and practicality, and balance today with tomorrow.
evidence_signals: Raised quality or performance with measured results
Chose a simple, practical solution over a clever one
Considered long-term maintainability alongside short-term delivery

principles.name: Get it Done
principles.description: Results matter. Work hard and smart, execute precisely and accountably while staying nimble, and follow through on commitments.
evidence_signals: Delivered on a commitment despite obstacles
Describes concrete execution steps and results, not intentions
Adapted plans quickly when conditions changed

principles.name: Own It
principles.description: Build the product and company as if it were yours. Take initiative, step up to own issues, and when you make a mistake, own it, fix it and learn.
evidence_signals: Took ownership of a problem outside their formal scope
Owned a mistake, fixed it and changed something afterwards
Uses 'I' clearly for own decisions

principles.name: Make Each Other The Best
principles.description: Treat people with kindness and respect, collaborate inclusively, give and ask for help and feedback, and teach and learn every day.
evidence_signals: Helped teammates grow or asked for help when needed
Gave or received constructive feedback and acted on it
Brought people and ideas together across teams

principles.name: Embrace Each Other's Differences
principles.description: Accept and appreciate people from every walk of life, stay mindful that others have different experiences, and use differences as a strength.
evidence_signals: Worked effectively with people of very different backgrounds or views
Adjusted own approach after understanding another perspective

rounds.name: Initial screen (recruiter or hiring manager)
rounds.notes: Official careers page: a 30-minute call about the candidate's technical background; the first conversation may be with the future manager. Third-party guides add a values and motivation check.

rounds.name: Technical interview
rounds.notes: Official: 60-minute coding and/or system design interviews with live coding. Some candidates report a 2-hour screen with one coding and one design part. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.notes: Panel coding round; roughly LeetCode medium with database or systems twists. Snowflake's AI guidance says at least one coding round may be in person. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Data infrastructure focus: query engines, storage, caching, multi-tenancy, security. Interviewers expect clarifying questions and follow up on trade-offs.

rounds.name: Expertise
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior engineer from the hiring team
rounds.notes: Official panel round. Team-specific: coding, system design, or a deep dive into database internals, a language or framework, or the candidate's own projects.

rounds.name: Tech Talk presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of engineers from the team
rounds.notes: Official: a 30-minute Tech Talk may be included depending on level and role. Guides report it for IC3 and above: present a past project, then answer questions.

rounds.name: Behavioral and collaboration
rounds.notes: Official panel includes behavioral and collaboration interviews. Ownership, teamwork, disagreement and mistakes; reflects Snowflake values.

rounds.name: Cross-functional
rounds.interviewer_role: People from several partner teams (engineering, product, sales)
rounds.notes: Reported by two guides for IC5 and above; each interviewer brings questions from their own department.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, why Snowflake and fit for the team. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager deep dive
rounds.notes: Deep questions on a product the candidate launched: roadmap, trade-offs, UX, what they would do differently. Interviewers double-click on details.

rounds.name: Presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of product and engineering leaders
rounds.notes: Reported by Prepfully and a Blind thread: present past work or career story, then defend choices (why this approach, what to cut if scope halved).

rounds.name: Strategy case
rounds.notes: A generic PM or customer scenario with technical follow-ups; scoping and clarifying first is expected. Classic consumer product-sense cases are rare.

rounds.name: Technical / domain
rounds.notes: Conversational fluency on cloud and data systems; more depth for senior and technical PM roles. Some teams skip it.

rounds.name: Behavioral
rounds.notes: Ownership, wrong decisions, disagreements with engineering.

rounds.name: Cross-functional
rounds.interviewer_role: Partner from engineering, security or go-to-market
rounds.notes: Aligning teams with conflicting goals and managing stakeholders.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background and motivation for Snowflake. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen (SQL)
rounds.notes: Live SQL: window functions, self-joins, consecutive-day problems, semi-structured data. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: SQL and query performance deep dive
rounds.notes: How the engine plans queries; pruning and clustering rather than indexes; diagnosing queries that slow as tables grow.

rounds.name: Data system design
rounds.notes: Pipelines that mix streaming and historical data, incremental loads, cost and reliability trade-offs.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.notes: Python, Java or C++ data structures, depending on team. ML roles add ML, statistics and applied AI topics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Behavioral
rounds.notes: Customer-first thinking, ownership and building at scale.

rounds.name: Initial screen (recruiter or hiring manager)
rounds.notes: Background and the programs the candidate ran. Based on the official general process; no TPM-specific official loop is published.

rounds.name: Technical / system design
rounds.notes: Candidate reports mention system design prompts and security or compliance programs (for example a GDPR plan for a security TPM).

rounds.name: Program execution
rounds.notes: Scope creep, delays, a critical bug just before release, timeline changes and their impact.

rounds.name: Behavioral and cross-functional
rounds.notes: A program that went badly, failures and lessons, working with engineering and product.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Pre-sales background, platforms sold with or against, territory. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Approach to technical sales, demos and complex enterprise deals.

rounds.name: Technical interview
rounds.notes: SQL, Snowflake architecture, data integration scenarios and light coding or API work; not LeetCode style.

rounds.name: Demo / case presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel: SE manager, senior SE and account executive
rounds.notes: Candidates get a customer scenario (about a week to prepare per one report), then demo and handle objections live.

rounds.name: Sales team panel
rounds.notes: How the AE and SE split a deal, pressure to overpromise, lost deals.

rounds.name: Regional leadership final
rounds.notes: Career direction and fit with a fast-paced sales culture.

question_patterns.pattern: A mistake the candidate made, how they owned and fixed it, and what they changed
A project that needed several teams to finish and how the candidate made the collaboration work
A time the candidate made a system faster or more reliable and proved it with numbers
A project the candidate drove independently from ambiguity to result
How the candidate's past experience lines up with the company's values, with specific examples
Walk through a product or system the candidate launched, then defend roadmap and design trade-offs under follow-up
Design part of a cloud data warehouse (query engine, storage format, metadata, cache) for very large data
Design isolation, scaling and security for many customers sharing a cloud data platform
Explain a core database concept (storage layout, indexing, concurrency, consensus) and its trade-offs
Propose a new product or feature for a data platform entering a new workload or market
Improve the experience of a technical persona (data engineer, analyst) using the platform
An enterprise customer makes an unusual request or reports a problem the metrics do not show; scope it, investigate and decide, with technical follow-ups
Present a past technical project, then defend design choices, alternatives rejected and what would change at larger scale
Diagnose and fix analytical queries or pipelines that degrade as data volume grows
Design a pipeline that combines streaming and historical data with correctness, cost and freshness trade-offs
A program hit a delay, scope change or late critical bug; how the candidate re-planned, communicated and protected the key outcome
Two teams or functions had conflicting goals (for example security versus latency) and the candidate brought them to a decision
A time the candidate had to tell a customer or partner about a limitation or resist pressure to overpromise

question_patterns.theme: Customer demo and proof of concept
question_patterns.pattern: Plan a demo or proof of concept for a customer scenario, tailored to its audience, with success criteria and objection handling

sample_questions.question: Design a system that ingests events with timestamps and organizes them so they can be retrieved quickly, for example by time range.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify volume, query patterns (time range, by key, latest N), retention and ordering guarantees. Discuss in-memory structures (sorted maps, skip lists) for one node, then time-partitioned storage with indexes, buffering and compaction for scale. Handle late or out-of-order events and hot partitions. State read versus write trade-offs and complexity of each operation.

looking_for: How you clarify query patterns before choosing structures
Whether you scale from one node to many
strong_signals: Covers sorted structures, time partitioning, indexes and compaction
Handles late events and hot partitions and states operation costs
watch_outs: Ignoring out-of-order data
No read versus write trade-off

sample_questions.question: Design a cloud-native SQL query engine that can run queries over petabytes of data.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Separate storage (columnar files on object storage with metadata such as min/max per file) from elastic compute. Walk the query path: parse, optimize (pruning, predicate pushdown, join order), distribute plan fragments to workers, exchange data, aggregate results. Cover skew and stragglers, caching, spilling to disk, failure retry, and concurrency between workloads. Explain why each choice fits analytical workloads.

looking_for: Whether you understand separated storage and compute
How you walk a query from parsing to results
strong_signals: Covers pruning, pushdown, distributed plans and data exchange
Handles skew, spilling, retries and competing workloads
watch_outs: Generic boxes with no query path
Ignoring stragglers and failures

sample_questions.question: Design resource management for a multi-tenant data platform with isolation between customers and automatic scaling.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify isolation needs (performance, security, cost). Compare dedicated compute per tenant versus shared pools with quotas. Cover admission control, queuing, autoscaling signals and cool-down, noisy-neighbor protection, and billing/metering. Discuss cold-start latency versus cost and how to fail safely.

looking_for: How you balance isolation, cost and scaling
Whether you protect customers from noisy neighbors
strong_signals: Compares dedicated and shared compute with quotas
Covers admission control, autoscaling signals and metering
watch_outs: Ignoring cold-start latency versus cost
No plan for failing safely

sample_questions.question: Design a distributed cache for query results, including how to invalidate entries when the data changes.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the cache key (normalized query plus data versions of referenced tables plus user context such as role). Invalidate by version change rather than by scanning. Cover placement, size limits and eviction, consistency guarantees, security (results must respect access rights), and hit-rate metrics. Discuss when caching is not worth it.

looking_for: How you define cache keys and invalidation
Whether cached results respect access rights
strong_signals: Invalidates by data version rather than scanning
Covers eviction, consistency, hit rate and when not to cache
watch_outs: Serving cached results to users with different permissions
Stale results with no versioning plan

sample_questions.question: Compare columnar and row-based storage. When would you choose each?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Row storage suits transactional workloads with point reads and writes of whole records. Columnar storage suits analytics: reads only needed columns, compresses well, enables vectorized execution, but makes single-row updates costly. Mention hybrid approaches and how micro-partitions with metadata enable pruning. Give a concrete example of each.

looking_for: Whether you know when each storage layout fits
How clearly you explain the trade-offs
strong_signals: Links row storage to transactions and columnar to analytics
Gives a concrete example and mentions pruning or hybrids
watch_outs: Saying one is simply better
No mention of update cost for columnar

sample_questions.question: Design a data security and governance system for a data platform.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover identity and authentication, role-based and attribute-based access control, row and column level policies, masking of sensitive fields, encryption at rest and in transit with key management, audit logging, data classification and lineage. Discuss performance cost of policy checks and how to manage policies at scale for many tenants.

looking_for: How broadly you cover access, protection and audit
Whether you think about policy cost at scale
strong_signals: Covers role and attribute access, row and column policies and masking
Includes encryption, key management, audit logs and lineage
watch_outs: Stopping at authentication
Ignoring the performance cost of policy checks

sample_questions.question: Design a video sharing service like YouTube, with focus on the caching layer.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Outline upload, transcoding, storage and metadata quickly, then go deep on caching: CDN for video segments, application cache for metadata and popular lists, cache keys, TTLs, invalidation on updates, and handling viral spikes. Quantify read/write ratios and storage. Discuss cost versus latency trade-offs.

looking_for: Whether you go deep on caching after a quick outline
How you handle viral traffic
strong_signals: Uses a CDN for video segments and app caches for metadata
Quantifies read and write ratios and weighs cost against latency
watch_outs: Spending the whole time on upload and transcoding
No invalidation or TTL plan

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you made a mistake.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real mistake with consequences. Say plainly what you did wrong, how you told others, how you fixed it, and what you changed to prevent a repeat. Snowflake's 'own it, fix it, learn from it, move on' wording fits this structure. Pitfall: a fake mistake or blaming others.

looking_for: Whether you own a real mistake plainly
How you fix it and prevent a repeat
strong_signals: Says what you did wrong and how you told others
Names the change you made afterwards
watch_outs: A fake or trivial mistake
Blaming others

sample_questions.question: Describe an experience where you had to collaborate across teams to get a project done.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the goal and why other teams were needed. Show how you aligned priorities, handled dependencies and disagreements, and kept communication clear. Give credit to others and state the delivered result. Pitfall: describing only meetings, not outcomes.

looking_for: How you align teams with different priorities
Whether you keep communication clear through dependencies
strong_signals: Shows how you handled a disagreement between teams
Credits others and states the delivered result
watch_outs: Describing meetings, not outcomes
No clear role for you

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a project you owned and led independently.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show the ambiguity you started with, how you defined the plan, made decisions, and kept it moving without being told. Quantify the result and name what you would do differently. Make your own role distinct from the team's.

looking_for: How you handle ambiguity without direction
Whether you drive decisions yourself
strong_signals: Shows how you defined the plan and kept it moving
Quantifies the result and names what you would change
watch_outs: Blurring your role with the team's
No measurable outcome

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you optimized a system for performance.
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the baseline and target with numbers. Explain how you profiled and found the real bottleneck, options you considered, the change you made and its trade-offs, and the measured result. Mention how you prevented regressions. Pitfall: optimizing without measuring.

looking_for: Whether you measure before you optimize
How you find the real bottleneck
strong_signals: States the baseline, target and measured result
Explains options, trade-offs and how you prevent regressions
watch_outs: Optimizing without measuring
No numbers

sample_questions.question: How does your experience align with Snowflake's values?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Know the values (for example Put Customers First, Own It, Get it Done). Pick two that truly fit you and give a short, specific story for each. Avoid listing all values. Interviewers look for authenticity and evidence, not slogans.

looking_for: Whether you know the company's values
Whether your fit is real and backed by evidence
strong_signals: Picks two values with a short, specific story for each
Sounds authentic, not rehearsed
watch_outs: Listing every value
Slogans with no stories

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a product you launched and your role in its roadmap, trade-offs and design.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give context, then your specific decisions: what went on the roadmap and why, what you cut, a key trade-off and its data, and how you worked with engineering and design. Expect the interviewer to double-click on details, so pick something you know deeply. End with results.

looking_for: How you make roadmap and design trade-offs
Whether you know your work in depth
strong_signals: Explains what you cut and the data behind a key trade-off
Shows how you worked with engineering and design, and the results
watch_outs: Picking a project you cannot go deep on
No results

sample_questions.question: Explain a recent project in technical depth: what you built, why, and what you would change.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover the problem, architecture, your part, the hardest technical decision, and measurable outcome. Be honest about weaknesses in the design. Match the depth to the role; for this company, data and performance details are welcome.

looking_for: How deep your technical understanding goes
Whether you can critique your own design
strong_signals: Covers the architecture, your part and the hardest decision
Gives a measurable outcome and honest weaknesses
watch_outs: Staying at a high level
Claiming the design had no flaws

sample_questions.question: If you could make Snowflake better, what would you change?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick one persona (for example data engineer or admin) and a concrete pain you can back up (cost visibility, onboarding, pipelines). Explain why it matters to customers and the business, propose a solution with MVP scope, and define a success metric. Show you know the product and its competitors. Pitfall: vague 'make it faster'.

looking_for: Whether you know the product and its users
How you prioritize one concrete pain
strong_signals: Picks a persona and a pain you can back up
Proposes a small first scope and a success metric
watch_outs: A vague 'make it faster'
No awareness of competitors

sample_questions.question: Give a 30-minute talk on a past technical project, then answer the panel's questions about your design choices.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a project you owned with real technical depth. Structure it: problem and constraints, architecture, your specific decisions, alternatives you rejected and why, results with numbers, and what you would change. Keep slides light and leave time for questions. In Q&A, answer directly, admit unknowns, and reason out loud about how the design would behave at larger scale or under failure.

looking_for: Whether you can explain your own work clearly to engineers
How you defend design choices under questions
strong_signals: Separates your decisions from the team's and names rejected options
Gives measured results and honest weaknesses
watch_outs: Running over time and leaving no room for questions
Getting defensive when a choice is challenged

sample_questions.question: Design authentication and authorization for a large web application.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify users, clients and threat model. Separate authentication (password plus MFA, SSO through SAML or OIDC, session or token handling, rotation and revocation) from authorization (roles, attributes, resource ownership). Cover where checks run, caching of permission decisions and its staleness risk, audit logs, rate limiting and lockout, secrets management, and key rotation. Discuss latency cost of checks and how the design scales across services.

looking_for: Whether you separate authentication from authorization
How you handle revocation and permission caching
strong_signals: Covers SSO, MFA, tokens, roles and audit logs
Weighs the latency of checks against freshness of permissions
watch_outs: Stopping at a login form
No plan to revoke sessions or rotate keys

sample_questions.question: How do you handle a disagreement with a teammate about a technical approach?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Use a real example. Show that you first understood the other view, then moved the debate to evidence: data, a prototype, or agreed criteria. Explain how the decision was made, how you committed to it even if it was not your option, and the result. Name what the disagreement taught you about working with that person.

looking_for: Whether you argue with evidence rather than opinion
Whether you commit once a decision is made
strong_signals: Restates the other view fairly
Shows commitment to the final decision and the outcome
watch_outs: A story where you were simply right
Escalating before trying to resolve it

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a product decision you made that turned out to be wrong.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real decision with visible cost. Explain the information you had and why the choice looked right then, the signal that showed it was wrong, how quickly you raised it, and what you did to correct course. Close with what you changed in how you decide, such as earlier validation or clearer kill criteria.

looking_for: Whether you own a real wrong call
How fast you noticed and corrected it
strong_signals: Explains the reasoning at the time and the signal that it was wrong
Names a lasting change in how you decide
watch_outs: Blaming the data or another team
A decision that was not really wrong

sample_questions.question: A large customer asks for a dedicated network path that only they would use. How do you respond?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start by finding the real need: security, compliance, latency or predictability. Check how many other customers share it and what existing options (private connectivity, dedicated tiers) already cover. Weigh revenue and strategic value against build and operating cost, margin impact and precedent. Recommend a path, such as a standard offering that solves the need or a scoped exception with clear terms, and say how you would measure success.

looking_for: Whether you clarify the underlying need first
How you balance one customer against the platform
strong_signals: Considers existing options and how many customers share the need
Weighs margin, operating cost and precedent before recommending
watch_outs: Saying yes or no without asking why
Ignoring the technical cost of a one-off

sample_questions.question: Customers in one region report slow performance, but your dashboards look normal. How do you investigate?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Take the reports seriously and get specifics: which workloads, times, clients and networks. Question the dashboards: aggregation hiding a tail, missing client-side or network metrics, sampling. Form hypotheses (regional network path, a dependency, a recent release, data skew) and test them with segmented metrics and customer traces. Communicate with the customers while you investigate, then fix the gap in monitoring so it shows next time.

looking_for: Whether you trust customer reports over averages
How you structure hypotheses
strong_signals: Questions what the dashboards measure, such as tail latency
Segments by region, workload and release, and fixes the monitoring gap
watch_outs: Dismissing the reports because metrics look fine
Jumping to one cause without testing

sample_questions.question: How would you weigh reliability against cost when deciding on cross-region failover for a cloud service?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from customer requirements: recovery time and data-loss targets per tier, and contractual commitments. Compare options: backups with restore, warm standby, active-active, with their cost, complexity and consistency implications. Tie the choice to the cost of downtime for customers and the business. Mention testing failover regularly and offering higher tiers to customers who need more.

looking_for: Whether you start from recovery targets
How you link technical options to business cost
strong_signals: Compares standby and active-active with cost and consistency
Mentions failover testing and tiered offerings
watch_outs: Choosing maximum reliability with no cost view
Not knowing what failover options exist

sample_questions.question: A security requirement adds latency that breaks another team's service-level targets. How do you resolve it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Bring both teams to shared facts: the actual risk the control addresses and the measured latency impact. Look for options that keep the protection with less cost: async checks, caching, scoping to sensitive paths, or optimizing the control. If a trade-off remains, frame it for the right decision maker with clear risk and impact, then communicate and track the outcome. Show you kept both teams' trust.

looking_for: How you turn a conflict into shared facts
Whether you find options before escalating
strong_signals: Quantifies both the risk and the latency impact
Proposes options that keep protection and frames the remaining trade-off
watch_outs: Picking a side without data
Escalating immediately

sample_questions.question: Queries on a table that grew from about 10 GB to 2 TB have become slow. How would you diagnose and fix this?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Look at the query profile first: bytes scanned versus partitions pruned, spilling, join explosion, skew. If filters no longer prune, reconsider clustering on common filter columns. Check for poor join order, exploding joins and SELECT *. Consider pre-aggregation or materialized results, incremental processing, and right-sizing compute. Measure before and after, and weigh compute and maintenance cost of each fix.

looking_for: Whether you diagnose before tuning
How well you understand pruning and clustering
strong_signals: Reads the query profile for scanned bytes, pruning, spills and skew
Weighs clustering, pre-aggregation and compute size by cost
watch_outs: Only saying 'use a bigger warehouse'
Talking about indexes as if it were a row store

sample_questions.question: Design a pipeline that combines real-time point-of-sale data with historical sales data for reporting.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify freshness, volume, late data and consumers. Ingest events continuously into a raw layer, deduplicate with idempotent keys, and merge incrementally into curated tables alongside batch-loaded history. Handle late and corrected transactions, schema changes, and slowly changing dimensions. Cover data quality checks, monitoring, backfills, and cost of keeping data fresh versus batch windows.

looking_for: How you reconcile streaming and batch data
Whether you plan for late and corrected records
strong_signals: Uses idempotent incremental merges and a raw-to-curated flow
Covers quality checks, backfills and the cost of freshness
watch_outs: Ignoring duplicates and late data
No monitoring or backfill plan

sample_questions.question: How would you handle a major delay in a program you are running?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Find the cause and real impact fast, then tell stakeholders early with facts and options rather than waiting for certainty. Re-plan: cut or phase scope, add or move resources, run work in parallel, and protect the outcome that matters most. Agree the new plan with engineering, product and leadership, track it visibly, and fix the planning gap that let the delay surprise you.

looking_for: How early and honestly you communicate
Whether you re-plan around the key outcome
strong_signals: Brings options, not just bad news
Fixes the planning gap that caused the surprise
watch_outs: Hiding the delay until the deadline
Only asking for more people

sample_questions.question: Describe a hard technical challenge you worked through and how its lessons would apply at Snowflake.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a challenge with real complexity and explain it simply. Show your role: how you organized people, dependencies and decisions, and which trade-offs you weighed. Give the result with numbers. Then connect the lesson to Snowflake's world, such as reliability at scale, multi-cloud operations, or coordinating many engineering teams.

looking_for: Whether you understand the technical problem yourself
How you connect the lesson to the company
strong_signals: Explains the challenge simply and your part in solving it
Links the lesson to scale, reliability or cross-team work
watch_outs: Staying vague about the technical details
A generic lesson with no link to the role

sample_questions.question: Plan a demo of the platform for a global enterprise that is modernizing its data estate.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with discovery: business goals, current architecture, pains, decision makers and competitors. Pick two or three use cases that map to those pains and build a story around the customer's data, not a feature tour. Tailor depth to the audience: business value for executives, hands-on detail for engineers. Prepare for likely objections such as migration risk and cost, and end with clear next steps.

looking_for: Whether you start from discovery rather than features
How you tailor the story to the audience
strong_signals: Maps a few use cases to the customer's stated pains
Anticipates objections and ends with next steps
watch_outs: A feature tour with no customer story
One depth for every audience

sample_questions.question: How would you approach a competitive proof of concept against another data platform vendor?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Agree success criteria with the customer up front: workloads, performance, cost, security and ease of use, with measurable exit criteria and a fixed timeline. Keep scope tight and say what is out of scope. Pick tests that reflect real workloads, play to real strengths, and be honest about gaps. Track progress with the account team and present results in the customer's terms.

looking_for: Whether you set measurable exit criteria
How you control scope
strong_signals: Agrees criteria and timeline with the customer first
Uses real workloads and is honest about gaps
watch_outs: Open-ended scope
Attacking the competitor instead of proving value

sample_questions.question: During a customer's proof of concept, compute spend spikes overnight. How do you find the cause?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Look at usage history by warehouse, user and query to find when and where the spike started. Check for runaway or repeated queries, scheduled tasks, auto-resume and auto-suspend settings, oversized compute, and failed retries. Fix the cause, then add guardrails such as resource monitors, budgets and alerts. Explain it to the customer plainly and agree how to prevent repeats.

looking_for: How systematically you trace usage
Whether you add guardrails afterwards
strong_signals: Breaks spend down by warehouse, user, query and time
Adds monitors or budgets and explains it plainly to the customer
watch_outs: Guessing a cause without looking at usage
Hiding the issue from the customer

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time a salesperson pushed you to promise something the product could not do.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the deal and the pressure. Show how you kept the promise honest: you explained the limitation to the account executive privately, found what the customer actually needed, and offered a workaround, roadmap context with care, or a partner option. Give the outcome for the deal and the relationship, and what you agreed with the sales team for next time.

looking_for: Whether you stay honest under sales pressure
How you keep the partnership with the account executive
strong_signals: Finds the customer's real need and offers a truthful alternative
Keeps trust with both the customer and the seller
watch_outs: Overpromising to win the deal
Undermining the seller in front of the customer

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Software Engineer I. Delivers well-defined tasks with strong coding fundamentals and guidance from senior engineers.
Software Engineer II. Owns features independently within a team.

Senior Software Engineer (postings ask about 5-6+ years). Owns projects end to end from design through testing and careful production rollout, runs services in production, solves hard performance problems, and mentors junior engineers.

Upper senior (Senior Software Engineer II on Levels.fyi; some sources call it Staff). Owns large components, designs next-generation architecture for a team's area and promotes good practices across the organization.

Principal Software Engineer I (postings ask about 10+ years). Plans and leads complex technical projects across many teams, acts as technical leader on critical cross-functional work, and mentors others.

Principal Software Engineer II (postings ask about 14+ years). Owns the technical vision for a major layer of the platform, such as data transformation processing, and sets direction for several teams.
About 7+ years. Owns and drives key cross-functional, often global programs to completion, maps dependencies and risks, and brings data-driven technical judgment to engineering and product decisions.

persona.tone: Professional and conversational; the first call may be a relaxed chat with the future manager, later rounds are focused and technical
persona.pace: Opens with one broad question, then double-clicks with layered follow-ups on the candidate's own answers
persona.pushback_style: Asks why one option over another, what would have changed your mind, and for data-system specifics, performance numbers and database internals
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions; Snowflake invites questions at every stage

case_style.notes: PM cases are strategy or customer scenarios on a cloud data platform (an unusual customer request, a regional performance complaint) with technical follow-ups, often after a presentation; scoping first is expected and estimation is rarely reported. Solution engineer cases are prepared customer demos and proof-of-concept plans with objection handling.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the eight values match on the official About page and the Code of Conduct, and job postings ask candidates to share them, but no public source says how they are scored in interviews. 'Embrace Each Other's Differences' is weighted lower because it is rarely probed directly.

loop_structure: the SWE loop follows Snowflake's official engineering process (30-minute screen, 60-minute technical interviews, 3-5 panel sessions, optional 30-minute Tech Talk). Round order varies by team. PM, data_ml, tpm and other (solution engineer) loops come from third-party guides and Blind threads only; the TPM loop is the thinnest (no TPM-specific process write-up found) and ML engineer rounds could not be checked because Interview Query returned HTTP 429.

question_patterns: the two PM sample questions sourced only to the Interview Query PM guide (streaming analytics product, data engineer developer experience) and the 'most innovative idea' question were removed because the guide still returned HTTP 429 on 2026-10-28; the developer-experience pattern stays as a pattern only. TPM questions rest on single question pages from Prepfully and InterviewPal.

bar_by_level: SWE scope comes from Snowflake job postings (Senior about 6+ years, Principal I about 10+, Principal II about 14+) read through job-board mirrors because careers.snowflake.com job pages did not render for the fetcher. Postings use only Senior and Principal titles; IC4 is now mapped to senior (Levels.fyi lists it as Senior Software Engineer II in some tables and Staff in others). PM levels have no public scope text and are not listed.

persona: based on the official note that the first call may be with the hiring manager and on several guides and a Blind thread that agree on layered 'double-click' follow-ups; no official description of interviewer style.

scoring_weights: derived from the evaluation areas Snowflake publishes for engineering (live coding and system design, role expertise, behavioral and collaboration, Tech Talk communication) plus guides that agree on database internals and ownership; the numbers are our estimate.
case_style: PM case format rests on Prepfully's PM guide and one Blind thread; solution engineer cases on CleverPrep and a Blind thread. No official case guidance.
